leo.central_question: Why does a straight straw look bent in a glass of water — and why does a swimming pool always look shallower than it really is?
leo.essential_idea: Light bends when it crosses from one transparent material to another because it changes speed at the boundary.

curiosity_hook.phenomenon: A straight metal rod pushed into a clear glass of water appears sharply broken at the water surface — as if it snapped. Pulled out: perfectly straight.
curiosity_hook.why_surprising: The rod is rigid and cannot bend. Something else must have changed.
curiosity_hook.opening_image: Close-up: a straight ruler enters water at an angle. At the water surface, the ruler appears to snap — the underwater half is displaced sideways. The glass is crystal clear.

common_misconceptions.statement: Light travels at the same speed in all transparent materials
common_misconceptions.why_believable: Light travels at 300,000 km/s — it seems impossible that glass or water could slow something so fast.

common_misconceptions.statement: The bent appearance is because water distorts vision like a wavy mirror
common_misconceptions.why_believable: Water surfaces ripple and distort reflections — students generalize this to all water-vision effects.

observation_sequence: A laser beam enters a rectangular glass block at an angle. Inside: beam bends toward the perpendicular at entry surface.
Beam exits the other side: bends away from the perpendicular. Exiting beam is parallel to entering beam but displaced.
Laser aimed straight at glass (0° angle): no bending at all. Beam continues straight.
Laser enters water at increasing angles: at the critical angle, refracted beam runs along the surface. Beyond it: total reflection.

prediction_opportunities.moment: After seeing light bend toward normal when entering glass...
prediction_opportunities.question: When light exits glass back into air, which way will it bend?
options: It will not bend — returns to original direction
prediction_opportunities.why_wrong_options_feel_right: Option A feels symmetric and consistent. Option C feels right because 'returning to air should undo everything.'

concept_reveal.the_moment: Soldiers marching in formation hit a sandy beach at an angle — front row slows first, back rows still fast — formation pivots. Light does the same. The wave front that hits glass first slows first. The rest catches up and the direction changes.
concept_reveal.what_becomes_visible: Speed difference causes direction change. Bending is not mysterious — it is the natural result of one part of a wave slowing before another part.

candidate_memory_models.name: Soldiers on Sand
candidate_memory_models.description: Soldiers marching in formation on hard ground reach a sandy beach at an angle. First soldier hits sand and slows. Others still fast. Formation pivots toward the sand. This is exactly how light waves bend at a glass surface — the wavefront pivots because one side slows first.
candidate_memory_models.why_memorable: Kinesthetic and spatial — students can feel the pivot in their own body.
candidate_memory_models.accuracy_note: Represents Huygens wave model — fully accurate.

real_world_connections.example: Fishing in Muttukadu backwaters — fish is never where it appears
real_world_connections.connection_to_concept: Refraction makes fish appear displaced upward. Fisherman must aim below apparent position.

real_world_connections.example: Mirage on Rajiv Gandhi Salai on hot days — road appears wet
real_world_connections.connection_to_concept: Hot air layer near road refracts sky light — total internal reflection creates appearance of water.

real_world_connections.example: Optical fibers carrying internet across Tamil Nadu
real_world_connections.connection_to_concept: Total internal reflection traps light inside fiber — same principle as critical angle observed in experiment.

reflection_questions: A diamond sparkles more than glass. Both refract light. What property of diamond causes more sparkle?
If you were a fish looking up from underwater, would the entire above-water world appear compressed into a small circle? Why?
Optical fiber cables carry information as light pulses. How does total internal reflection make this possible?

memory_anchor.image_description: A perfectly straight straw in a glass of water, viewed from the side. The straw appears sharply broken at the water surface — the underwater half visibly displaced to the right. Crystal clear glass. Unmistakably bent straw.
memory_anchor.anchor_sentence: A straight straw looks broken in water — because light slows down and bends when it moves from water to air.
memory_anchor.cognitive_hook: The visual wrongness — straight object appears broken — creates cognitive dissonance. Every student has seen this with a spoon. Personal memory plus explanation equals strong encoding.

assessment_insight.understanding_vs_memorization: Memorization: Snell's law n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂. Understanding: Student predicts bending direction for any material pair, explains why pool appears shallow, calculates depth error, explains optical fiber.
assessment_insight.tn_board_pattern: 1-mark: Define refractive index. State Snell's Law. 3-mark: Explain total internal reflection with critical angle diagram. 5-mark: Refraction through glass slab or prism with diagram and all angles labeled.
assessment_insight.marks_tip: Always draw the normal line (dashed, perpendicular to surface) before drawing ray paths. Measure all angles from normal, never from surface — TN Board deducts marks for angles measured from surface.
